It is the first to which I wish to call attention. While the minister has skated round it and hinted at it, the fact remains that, while the bill may not be proclaimed this year, it is setting up the framework of what the government proposes shall take the place of the present wheat board. The wheat board will either be eliminated, if the government think conditions warrant such action, or be made inoperative as it was in 1936-37. There is no use thinking that the two schemes can operate side by side. If the wheat board is there, willing to pay a fixed price of 70 cents, and also give participation certificates which will enable the farmer to derive benefit from any increase in price, he is certainly not going to sell to any association of pools at an initial price of 60 cents. This legislation is clearly the government's alternative policy to a 100 per cent pool or even the type of pool that we have at the present time.
For that reason I must certainly oppose this measure. This is a fundamental issue. Perhaps the government would have been further ahead had they clearly said that the wheat board is no longer to be part of a permanent policy, but is to be used this year under difficult circumstances and to be eliminated as soon as possible and replaced by the type of system outlined in this bill.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Is the hon. member against cooperative marketing?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
I certainly am not, but I am very much against a system which is called cooperative marketing but is not cooperative marketing, and which will supplant the only thing we have had which has come reasonably close to cooperative marketing.

Cooperative Wheat Marketing

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: That is only the hon. member's idea.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
I point out further, as the minister himself said this afternoon, that it is not required under the legislation that there shall be one central selling agency; it will be possible to have a number of cooperatives or associations or pools each with a different selling agency. The minister envisages a time when they might finally centralize in one selling agency, but after the putting into operation of this bill there will probably be a great number of selling agencies all in competition with each other, with most disastrous results in terms of price and of the standard of living of the people.
While this may be called a bill to encourage cooperatives-although I think it is more likely to discourage them-certainly it will not encourage producers' cooperatives. I cannot see much coming from any cooperative in which groups of line elevator companies are included. I cannot envisage some of the large grain dealers and elevator companies listed this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture contributing very much over a long period to cooperation. I do not think the minister needed to travel all this long roundabout road to deal with the problem which he mentioned on February 16. He pointed out very properly that the present wheat legislation has not been equitable in its benefits; I think we all agree with that. But instead of throwing it away for something that is not nearly as good, we would much better have kept the wheat board with a fixed minimum price and participation certificates, and enacted legislation giving proper crop insurance to take care of those people who, because they had no crops, did not benefit under the Wheat Board Act. Early in the session a resolution favouring crop insurance was moved by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. McDonald) and passed by the house. I think most hon. members favour some type of crop insurance. These two projects together, the Wheat Board Act to take care of the man who has a crop, and a crop insurance scheme to take care of the man who has none, would have levelled out any inequalities. But this bill envisages throwing out the Wheat Board Act, which has perhaps done more to guarantee some measure of stability in western Canada than any other single agency in a good many years.
There is one other matter, which comes under Bill No. 89, but I do not want to take part in the discussion at that time. It seems to me that for products other than
wheat, rather than setting up these little associations and pools that are going to be difficult of operation and control from this distance, the government might well consider something similar to the natural products marketing legislation, with this difference, that there would be inserted a provision that it would become operative in each province only when that province passed enabling legislation. Legislation is already in operation in British Columbia, New Brunswick and I believe another province-

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Six provinces.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: It seems to me that it would not be very difficult, in view of the experience the minister has gained in the last few years, to draft a federal bill which would enable the respective provinces to fit into a gigantic cooperative scheme right across Canada that would respect the rights of both federal and provincial governments. I think that could be done, and I believe it would be very much better than trying to set up these associations and pools, which, in my opinion, will not only be unworkable but at the same time be so numerous and so lacking in uniformity as to be almost impossible of operation.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Definitions.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Is there any particular
reason for limiting an elevator company for the purposes of this bill, in paragraph (d), to a company operating or controlling 100 or more country elevators?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: The main reason has been given by almost every speaker who has taken the other side of the question. The suggestion has been made that there is an argument against having too many pools, and this provision does limit that number to fifteen, plus any others that may be organized into groups of at least 100. This could result in the formation of something like twenty pools. That would be the limit. If there were no provision of this kind there might be 153 pools.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Has the minister had any representation made to him in regard to discrimination against two or three firms at the head of the lakes and other private elevator interests which will not come under the bill?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Yes, I had a letter,
probably from the same company to which
Cooperative Wheat Marketing

the hon. member refers, the Fort William Terminal Elevator Company or some such name, suggesting that they might find it difficult to operate under the bill. I had the fullest possible inquiries made, and the opinion is that they could operate under this bill. I do not think there would be any great difficulty about entering into an agreement provided they could get their commission men organized to operate under a bill of this kind. The main difficulty would be a practical one. If a farmer pools his wheat he can have it all handled through the elevator. If he deals with a commission house, in all probability he would load over the platform. I can hardly conceive that any considerable number of farmers would want to shovel their wheat out of a wagon into a car and also back into the ends of the car in preference to putting it through an elevator under a pooling arrangement. I think those who do pool will put it through an elevator.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
What about the private
elevator operator? There is one at Pense, as the minister knows, another at Estevan and another at Wolseley. What is going to happen to these small fellows?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
They would operate
exactly as they did when the pools were in existence, Then they had an agreement with the central selling agency whereby they took delivery of the wheat of any farmer and delivered it to the pools. They would do the same under this legislation.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: They could deliver it to any of these companies?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: To any of the pools. They would make an arrangement with one pool and would deliver grain to that particular pool.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to retain the wheat board as the central selling agency of these pools?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
The wheat board, of course, is operating as a central selling agency now for all those who delivered under the wheat board method of marketing. Our experience during the years we have had the wheat board has been that there is very little delivery, if any, when the price is above the initial payment, probably for the reason given a few moments ago by the desk-mate of the hon. member, that the individual himself feels he does not really want to pool. I can hardly conceive of that individual entering into this pooling arrangement. If a man is not convinced that he can get better 
results over a term of years out of pooling than by following another method, he is not likely to continue to pool his grain.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
What benefit could you
get under the pooling arrangement that you could not get under the wheat board? In both instances you receive an initial payment and then the balance on the average over the year. I cannot see any advantage in this method.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Except that under this legislation you can get an organization similar to the pool you had previously. You can have a contract pool, but with the present wheat board you cannot have that.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
But surely the minister
will agree that when the government is guaranteeing a payment of only 60 cents, which means about 37 cents to the farmers, they cannot afford to pool their wheat. With all their expenses they cannot wait until the following spring for the balance. Whether or not they want to join such a pool they will not be able to do so under such a low guarantee.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Of course a man does not enter into a cooperative arrangement of this kind unless he is completely sold on the idea and feels that over a term of years he is going to make more money by this method. While there may be some truth in what the hon. member says, I think he will agree that my original statement was in accordance with the facts. That is, a man can put wheat in the ground and take it off again at the prices that have been discussed here. He cannot, of course, build up a home and continue existing year after year at that level, but he can pay the cost of putting the grain in the ground and threshing it.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Provided be has not to pay for any machinery.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
He pays for his
machinery in years when he makes some profit on his crop.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
This discussion has to do with section 2, but if I may be permitted I should like to ask a question in regard to section 3. From the question asked a moment ago I gather that the hon. member takes it that there is really a guaranteed price of 60 cents. That is not so under section 3. Does it not say there that it will be done by agreement, that the initial payment may not exceed 60 cents but may be less? I think that is a point which should be made perfectly clear.

Cooperative Wheat Marketing
Another question I should like to ask the minister is this:	The average sale price is
to be fixed in a manner to be prescribed by regulation; that is, the determination of what is the average sale price will be carried on in a manner to be determined by regulation. Does that mean by regulation as it is interpreted in a subsequent clause, by the government by order in council, or does it mean by a regulation of the pool itself?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Regulation by order in council.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Should not the principles
upon which that average price may be determined be set forth in the bill? As it is, it leaves wide open the matter of what will constitute an average price. Let me illustrate what I mean in a few words, if I may, because I do not wish to detain the committee. We will say that an initial price of 60 cents has been paid, less, of course, all charges including freight, commission to the agency and so on. In the first few months, as the minister intimated, there may be a drop, which is likely to be the case when the flush delivery comes on the market. Later on, in November, December, January or thereabouts, the price may rise. It is quite competent under subsection 2 of section 3 for those in charge to say that the man who delivers in the early part of the season shall not participate to the extent to which the person who delivers when prices are higher may participate. There is nothing to hinder them from determining that the principle which will fix the average price shall be on a dual basis. Some would participate on a scale fixed on a lower price, and some would participate on a scale fixed on a higher price; the whole matter would then become most confused, and a most discordant note would be introduced.
The section provides the decision of the minister shall be final, which, I should say, places the minister in a most unfair and awkward position. It would be much better if we could introduce into section 3 some principle similar to that which was worked under the old wheat board, where participation certificates were given. That is a principle which is known, which has operated and which has been accepted. That would be better than leaving the matter open, because one pool may have one form and another a different one. All of this is under agreement between the pools and the minister, and there is no determining principle in the measure to guide the minister or to indicate to the pools what their rights may be. That is the point I am trying to emphasize.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Would the hon. member leave the discussion of that until we reach section 3?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
I thought we were on
section 3.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Initial payments paid to selling agencies.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Section 3 reads in part:
(1) The minister may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, by agreement with any selling agency, undertake that if the average sale price of all wheat of any grade grown in a crop year delivered to the selling agency under one or more cooperative plans is less than a sum certain per bushel-
I would point out that the average sale price comes into that determination and, as the hon. member for Kootenay East knows, there are many grades of wheat. Speaking from memory, I believe there are forty-two different grades. Of course 60 cents is taken as the figure with which you start, but the sum certain for any particular grade is figured from that average. These questions with regard to regulation have to do largely with that matter, namely the matter of determining the relationship between 60 cents and the price of some other grade. Someone has to have the final say in a matter of that kind as to whether or not a company has kept the agreement, and the bill provides the minister shall have that final say.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: The minister has missed my point. My point is that the question of an average price was the gravamen of this section. What is the average price? From this bill, when it becomes law, no one can tell.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: They have to show from their accounts what the average sale price was.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
The minister says that, but the bill does not say it. Subsection 2 reads:
(2) The average sale price shall, for the purposes of this section, be computed after the sale prices realized by the selling agency have been adjusted, in a manner to be prescribed by regulation-
"In a manner to be prescribed by regulation," not "in a manner that is computed on the actuarial determination of price disclosed in the accounts of the company or pool." It does not say that. No principle is indicated. In my opinion, it leaves it in a confused and open condition.
Cooperative Wheat Marketing

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
I would point out, only in arguing the point, of course, that it states:
The average sale price shall, for the purpose of this section, be computed after the sale prices realized by the selling agency have been adjusted-

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: All right; it is all right to that point.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
And it continues:
-in a manner to be prescribed by regulation. . . .

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Exactly.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: And the regulation will simply set up the method by which that adjustment is to be made.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: True; but what method?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: "As if the wheat had been sold in store at Fort William." Some of that wheat may go to Vancouver, or some of it may go to a mill at another point. This section simply says that the value at that particular point shall be computed in relation to shipments of similar amounts of similar grain to Fort William. That cannot be put into legislation.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Well, I will not labour the point, but I submit that it is not dealt with in that way.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: That is the intention of it, and that is the way in which it was previously dealt with in the pools.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
In section 3, proceeding from the point where the hon. member for Kootenay East left off I read:
. . . there shall be paid to such selling agency the amount, if any, by which the initial payment together with storage, carrying and transportation charges and operating expenses exceeds the average sale price aforesaid.
My question is this: In the event of the wheat price going down and the farmer receiving the initial payment, who would pay the storage charges?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: It would be involved in the initial guarantee.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Who pays everything?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: But the initial guarantee may possibly be less than 60 cents.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: It may be less to the individual farmer. That is, the initial starting point may not be 60 cents.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
What price would he get, then? The farmer should know
that.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: I believe I dealt with that point when discussing the bill previously. However, from the experience of the pools it would work out about this way, that in the average year there would be about three cents required to take care of operating and storage costs. In one year of the operation of the pools the costs ran to about five cents. It is possible that if pools were starting to operate again under this bill, and if they started in a year like this they could start at only 55 cents, instead of 60 cents. Our hope is that when the bill comes into operation we shall be in a more favourable year than the present one. The wheat board is operating this year, in the manner in which it is, because of the emergency that exists. If we come to a time when people generally think an emergency does not require further operation of that kind, this bill might come into effect to cover a large percentage of the crop. Under those circumstances I would hope it would come into effect in a year when the price was much better than it is to-day, in which event, under this measure, we would enter into an agreement with a company to set up a reserve, which would make possible the payment of the full 60 cents. Instead of providing two or three cents or five cents below, they would provide a reserve above 60 cents, and that reserve would take care of carrying charges.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Until that reserve is built up, the farmer will receive 60 cents, minus handling, storage and transportation charges?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: He would have to, if it was set up in a year like this.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Then it would be considerably less.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Is there no possibility of increasing the minimum price of sixty cents? A price increase has already been made in the bill of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have here a resolution from the Alberta board of trade and agriculture, one paragraph of which reads:
If economic forces throughout the world were allowed free play, low grain prices would drive a large percentage of the producers in marginal areas in certain countries into other pursuits. Thus the present burdensome surplus would disappear. But no hope of any such natural adjustment may be entertained until competing countries discontinue subsidization.

Cooperative Wheat Marketing
That means, of course, countries like Britain and Germany, and as regards Britain the hon. member for Acadia mentioned this afternoon that 250,000 acres of grass lands would be cultivated there this year. We realize that substitutes are largely taking the place of many of the food products we produce, and others are subsidized in different countries. It must be remembered that our western grain growers have no other means of livelihood open to them than agriculture, and it is necessary to have some price fixed for wheat. It does seem to me that 60 cents is too low. If it could be raised to 70 cents I would appreciate this legislation more.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
On the second reading of the bill I tried to explain as fully as possible why it would not be advisable to set the advance higher than 60 cents in a bill of this kind, the chief reason being that we have already had experience in trying to maintain under the pooling system an initial payment that was at a level higher than the world price happened to be for the time being. We had that experience in 1929 and 1930, and it resulted in a loss of somewhere between 24 and 25 million dollars on wheat and coarse grains to the three western pools.
" I said this afternoon that I thought it would be agreed by all those who were interested in the pools at the time that the main reason for their difficulties was that they were not able to reduce their advance payment as rapidly as the world market price was falling. I think, too, it will be agreed by all those who have had experience with the pools that if they were to start to operate again they should operate from a price base as safe as one can make an advance payment of this kind. I read this afternoon from the opinion of the board of the largest of the three pools, the Saskatchewan pool, to the effect that while they are not prepared at the moment to say that they agree to 60 cents they are not asking us at this time to increase the 60 cents fixed by this bill. I think it would be wise to put the bill through the house with the price left as it is, and to have the bill discussed on that basis. There are some chances that the bill might operate in relation to the marketing of a portion of the crop this year, but that is not likely with the situation as it is now, and parliament may be in session again before the bill gets into operation. I think it would be well that the bill should go through with the 60 cents standing as it is, and if there is a real desire in western Canada to open up the pools we can discuss the matter from the point of view of a price that is absolutely safe from the point of view of the pools themselves.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: I should like the minister to explain the real object in putting the bill through at this session. He told us this afternoon that the legislation was not likely to operate this year, that the wheat board would continue, and he hoped that the market price would be higher before the bill was proclaimed. It may be several yeare before that happens, and I am wondering why the bill should be pressed through at this session.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
If it is several years
before the price goes higher we shall need to put many more things than this bill through the house, but our experience over the yeare would indicate that the price has been very close to the bottom this year.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Does the minister not
think that the board could take care of the situation just as effectively as the associations or pools proposed to be set up under this bill?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Of course there is a
considerable opinion in the western part of Canada, I do not say a majority opinion but a considerable opinion, that some agency, which is not of necessity controlled from the central parliament of Canada, should eventually be set up to handle the marketing of the grain of the three western provinces. The reason for that is that about 25 per cent of the population of Canada are involved in the production of western wheat, and it is difficult, except under emergent conditions, to handle, from the central government of Canada, an organization which would be at all times satisfactory to the people who are producing the crop. There are many who think we would be in a much better position so far as our grain is concerned-and the time may come when this will be the case-if we had an organization of producers from the area where the wheat is produced controlling the marketing of their own crop, and I consider a piece of legislation which makes that a possibility for the future is advisable.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Is any provision made for a grain firm withdrawing from one of these associations? One firm may go with twenty others to form one of these associations, find it unsatisfactory and want to withdraw. Is provision made for that?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
That provision would
be in the agreement between the companies themselves. If they get down below one hundred they would not be able to operate under this bill, but if there were 125, the agreement among the companies would take care of the situation my hon. friend suggests.
Cooperative Wheat Marketing

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
The minister continually
stresses the 825,000,000 loss in 1929. But at the beginning of the 1929 crop year the price was close to $1.50 a bushel, and it was only the faulty administration of our banking and monetary systems that put the pools and other organizations in the position in which they found themselves a little later.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: I am a little puzzled at the attitude of the minister on the question of price. Am I right in understanding that he takes the stand that the government would not be justified in setting a price which might entail a loss? In other words, he is opposed to giving the wheat growers a subsidy. The minister has referred to the loss which the wheat pools suffered, but I do not see how he can make such a comparison because the pools had no funds to draw upon. The government is in an entirely different position. Surely we realize that, on account of the fact that western Canada is suffering the penalties of monetary reaction, fiscal reaction and various other things, it is entitled to some form of compensation. Therefore I feel, and I think the government should feel, that the farmers of the west have a perfect right to a set price which may involve a loss to the government, simply to return to western Canada something equivalent to the cost of production.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
The government quite
agrees that some means has to be found of taking care of the difficulties which have resulted in western Canada from eight crop failures. In the past we have been taking care of that through the giving of relief and paying for that relief out of the treasury of Canada. We are providing, to an extent at least, in another piece of legislation which will come down in due course and will be discussed, for taking care of that problem. We are not attempting in this bill to take care of that problem. This bill is simply an attempt to set up the basis of a method of marketing wheat, and the attempt is being made to make that basis sound financially.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
The minister will agree
that Bill No. 63 will not in any way affect this bill. If prices go down to 20 or 30 cents a bushel, neither of these other bills will help at all.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: If wheat went down to 20 or 30 cents a bushel and this particular bill was in operation, it would take care of those who marketed under it to the extent of 60 cents a bushel.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
The street price would be
only about 37 cents if No. 1 at Fort William is 60 cents.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
My hon. friend
and other hon. members have said on two or three occasions that the average price would be 37 cents. They are gauging that because, they say, last year, with wheat on an 80-cent basis at Fort William it returned 57 cents to the farmer. But they surely know that if there had been no 80-cent basis this last year, the return to the farmer would not have been 37 cents, it would have been, at the lowest, 42 cents.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Because the
average price never got below 65 cents for the year, and therefore the price to the farmer would be the 23 cents under that, of which he speaks. Even if there had been no set price this last year, the world market price which was reflected back into Canada was an average of about 65 cents, and under a board they would not have got any wheat at 60 cents.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
That was because there
was a set price of 80 cents.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Not at all. Why did it not stop above that, then?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
If the committee would
allow me, I should like to ask a question with regard to section 2. I was unfortunately called out of the chamber.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
As regards section 2, I
wrote to the minister, but I did not have a chance to ask him, about the definition of elevator companies. I believe that some explanation was made, but perhaps he could in two or three sentences explain to me the position with regard to such a company as the Fort William Elevator Company, which has no country elevators. He understands the case, I believe.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Yes. That is a question, I believe, which was asked by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle with regard to the same company; I had just forgotten the name of it. I stated on that occasion that they wrote to me direct as well as to the leader of the opposition and apparently to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I have had the matter examined into carefully with the intention, had it been necessary, of bringing down an amendment, but I am informed that it is not necessary, that under the cooperative acts of

Cooperative Wheat Marketing
the provinces it would be possible for these groups which are interested to set up an organization under the first definition of cooperative, under a cooperative plan, to operate if they desire to do so under this bill. There would, of course, have to be a number of them somewhat similar to the number of elevators before it would be acceptable, but they could operate in that way.
There is a practical difficulty in connection with the matter, and it is this, that most of the pooling is done through elevators. When a man drives into a country elevator he simply dumps his wagon load into the pit and that is all he has to do. If he deals through a commission man, very likely he has to load over a platform; if he loads from the platform he shovels his wheat with a scoop into the car, and then he gets into the car and shovels it back into the end of the car.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Sometimes he gets better weight in that way.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Yes, sometimes he gets better weight, or he thinks he gets a better price. But if he is going to pool his wheat along with 10,000 other farmers, and 9.999 of them put their wheat through the elevator, he will not go to that extra work of shoveling his wheat into a car in order to pool it along with the other fellow and take the same price. In other words, that practical difficulty would probably result in very little wheat being pooled over the platform. There may be some way of overcoming that. A commission man does not necessarily have to buy over the platform; he can have his wheat put through an elevator by paying the charges of putting it through.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: The company seems to be afraid of being put out of business. Is it likely to be put out of business through this legislation?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Oh, no. There never was- at any time more than about 50 per cent of the wheat of western Canada handled through the pools, even when the pools were going at their strongest. I assume that this company was operating then-

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
-and probably got
wheat to the same extent as it gets it now. I think that if the pools were operating, at least half the wheat would probably be going through other channels.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Assuming that this bill is proclaimed and assuming that these cooperatives and pools are set up; what would be their relationship to the wheat board?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Well, of course the
wheat board might be constituted by agreement the central selling agency. So long as the wheat board was operating I assume it would be acceptable to all as the central selling agency.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: It would cease to be a buying agency?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: It would cease to take delivery of wheat?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: No, they would take delivery of pool wheat from these particular organizations. That is, that part of the wheat which went into an elevator to be pooled would be marketed by the wheat board; they would be the central selling agency.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: But they would not take wheat direct from the producer and issue participation certificates as the act now provides?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: The position would be this, that in all probability wheat would be above the set advance. That is to say, the set advance now in the bill which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has introduced is 70 cents. If the price were 75 cents, then all the elevator companies would be buying grain and getting delivery of grain from farmers at 75 cents; but they would be open at the same time to take pooled grain; the pooled grain would go to the wheat board, and the farmers would get the advantages of the participation certificates which are provided for in the wheat board bill, just the same as they did previously from the wheat pool. In other words, there is nothing in this 'bill to prevent the wheat board from being established as the central selling agency and everybody who enters into a pooling arrangement sending his grain to that organization.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
There is
nothing to guarantee it, though, in this bill?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: No, there is nothing to guarantee it; but there is nothing to prevent it, either.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Am I correct in assuming, from the remarks made by the minister a few minutes ago, that this bill will entirely eliminate the track buyer? The reason why I ask the question is that I have had some letters from track buyers, and they have that fear.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
No, this bill would not eliminate any grain dealer who can deal in grain now. It is purely a voluntary measure, and only farmers who desire to deal with the

Cooperative Wheat Marketing
pool would deliver to that particular organization; all others would deliver their grain just as they have been delivering it, to track buyers or anybody else.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Would the minister indicate the date when we may expect that the average sale price will be arrived at and when there will be payments subsequent to the initial payment? I think some date should be fixed whereby the farmer will know when he may expect subsequent payments.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: The " crop year " means a period of twelve months commencing on the 16th day of July in any year and ending on the 15th day of July in the following year. These settlements would be made just as they were under the provincial pool legislation, in the middle of the month of July.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: One final payment?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: No. There is provision made that there may be an interim payment, with the consent of council, or more than one interim payment, and then a final payment.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Let me come back to the question I was discussing with the minister. He suggested that the wheat board might become the central selling agency ?or these respective pools and cooperatives. If that were done-he does not give any guarantee that it will be done-while it would be in harmony with the statement he made earlier in the year in regard to the Turgeon commission's recommendation that the government should remain out of the grain business, I believe that most people in western Canada are anxious to know, and it would be fairer to all concerned if they were told, what the government has definitely in mind. Is the board merely to be held on to for another year because the situation is abnormal ; or is it to be kept in the background so that it may be resorted to and made operative in any year in which we are faced with a disastrous price drop; or is it to be eliminated altogether; or, as the minister has suggested, is it to become the central selling agency for these organizations-or, in other words, is the government going to remain partly in the business? The minister should make some statement with reference to the government's policy and the future operations of the wheat board.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
It is difficult on this
question as on many others to say very far in advance what government policy ought to be in relation to some particular features of the matter. In so far as the wheat board is concerned, it has been said on a number of

occasions that the board is necessary in order to deal with an emergent condition such as we have at present. That was stated a year ago and we continued the wheat board then. It has been stated again this year and we are continuing the wheat board for the handling of this year's crop. This particular piece of legislation which we are now putting on the statute books, as I have indicated on a number of occasions during these discussions, will probably not come into effect as long as the price remains at the level at which it has been during the last number of months. It is on the upgrade at the present time-it was 66 cents to-day-and there is a possibility that it may reach, some time during the next year, a level where all those interested, the producers and those who have been handling the grain by one method or another, might want, to sit down and discuss the question as to what would be the proper future policy with respect to the handling of our grain.
We have still in existence the wheat board under Bill No. 63. We have set up under this bill the possibilities of organization based upon the pooling idea, and there is, in the legislation which has been before the committee on agriculture during the past week or two, provision for the regulation of the grain trade as it has been operated since 1904. With all that legislation provided, along with the bill now before the committee, we shall be in a position to give every consideration necessary to the future handling policy for the marketing of wheat; and if it is considered wise by all those who enter into these discussions that the proper kind of selling agency to have is an agency operated under the direction of this government through the wheat board, then that possibility can be taken into account. On the other hand, if the western producers, because of the experience they have had with the whole handling of grain, feel that they would rather have some sort of central selling agency over which they will have absolute control as producers, then it will be possible to consider that point of view. But there are no possibilities that are headed off by the legislation before the house.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
It does not seem fair to the idea of orderly marketing that the wheat board should be used only on a falling market and be discarded for some other form of marketing the moment we get on to a rising market. I do not think any argument has been advanced by the minister or the government to show why it would not be possible to continue the wheat board and to continue taking delivery of wheat. If a rising market is to be expected, all the better;

Cooperative Wheat Marketing
but there is no reason why, during the period that the price goes above the guaranteed price, a reserve could not be built up. Provision could be made so that instead of the participation certificates giving back to the farmers all that accrues to them, a part be given back and the rest used to build up a reserve, so that when the price begins to drop again we will have a wheat board that will not make too great a drain upon the dominion treasury, a board that will not bring orderly marketing into disrepute.
One of the things we have been most unfair about with regard to the wheat board is this: It has been given a black eye because it has been used only in bad times. If it were a permanent policy it would commend itself to the people of eastern Canada as well as to those of the west. The people of eastern Canada have a wrong impression of the wheat board because it has been used only in bad times. I think the minister should give us the reasons that impel the government to desert the idea of the wheat board as a permanent policy. I do not believe the minister would say now that it was inequitable because only the farmer who has a crop gets a return. The crop bonus scheme will take care of that, and it is good supplementary legislation. At any rate, it has not been explained why the board as a permanent policy should not be continued.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
There is really only one reason why the wheat board might not be continued as a permanent means of marketing the crop of western Canada, and that is exactly the same reason why the pool was not continued beyond 1930. I explained that this afternoon. The pool was not continued beyond 1930 because we as farmers, we as pool signers, insisted on such a high initial payment for our wheat in 1929 and 1930 that the world market would not pay that price, with the result that the wheat pools lost between $24,000,000 and $25,000,000. We have had a similar experience with the wheat board this last year. Everyone knows that no one was satisfied last year when the price of wheat was set at 80 cents. No one expressed immediate satisfaction with that in western Canada-at least very few did. There was just as much agitation for 87 cents or higher one year ago as there is now for 80 cents or higher, and the government set 80 cents, which was a reduction of 7J cents.
There is only one reason why there is agitation to-day for doing away with the wheat board as a means of marketing the crop, and that is the fact that they paid out, through that marketing, something in the neighbourhood of $48,000,000 more than they could have got during the same period for the wheat they took in. The dominion as a whole, eastern Canada and western Canada alike, has taken the position that it is not too much to pay $48,000,000 to western Canada this year in order to assist in reestablishing the wheat growing area of western Canada. But everyone outside western Canada, and most of those who live in the west, most of the farmers themselves, have criticized the fact that a large proportion of that $48,000,000 went to the people who needed it least in order to reestablish themselves, and the people who certainly needed it got very little or nothing of it. That has been the criticism.
In answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Weyburn I venture to say that no government would be permitted to carry on in this country very long which would set up that policy as a permanent method of dealing with marketing the wheat of western Canada. It is with a view to establishing a sounder basis for the marketing of the wheat of western Canada, a basis that will be acceptable to the western fanners themselves as a whole, that will be satisfactory to business people in general throughout Canada and acceptable to agricultural people in other parts of Canada, that we are attempting to set up something which is at least more sound than the method followed last year.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: Is it not a fact that if the price of wheat is set by the Minister of Trade and Commerce at 70 cents, as proposed, if in October it goes up two or three cents, gets over 70 cents, the board will get no wheat so far as this year's crop is concerned [DOT] it might just as well go out of existence? The only way whereby you could get the farmers of western Canada to deliver their wheat to the board would be by regimentation and compulsion.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Well, that has been the experience up to date. It is not the fact that the government, whether this or any past government, has a particular line of policy that brings about the delivery of wheat to the board; it is the attitude of the farmer himself. When the previous government brought in their grain board legislation in 1935 they made delivery compulsory, and they met with some opposition in trying to put the compulsory measure through this house. When the bill finally went through it was made voluntary, with a set price and the provision that the government take the loss on sales below that price, and participation certificates issued for any surplus above that price. The government gets no wheat unless the market price
Cooperative Wheat Marketing

is below the established minimum or established advance. In this year, when the market price has 'been continuously below the advance price, the government gets all the wheat, which puts all other parts of the grain trade out of existence. But in a year like last year when the average price was $1.31, even had the government taken no action at all the wheat board would not have got any wheat, they would have been sitting on the side lines. It goes without saying, I think, that this house would not be satisfied with setting up and paying for two sets of organizations in Canada to handle grain, only one of which functions. We should have some system which at least gives the farmer when he comes to the elevator a choice to say what he wants to do.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: What the minister says now pretty well contradicts what he said this afternoon. He pointed out then that often the farmer goes to the elevator, decides he does not want to sell his wheat, but gets an advance on it. Here is the very same thing.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
The hon.
member does not even wait to hear what I am going to say.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: You say it is the same thing; I say no.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
The hon.
member comes from a farming community; no doubt we shall all be glad to hear what he has to say later, without his interrupting someone else.
There is no guarantee that because the price is higher than the fixed minimum the farmers will not deliver their wheat to the pool. As a matter of fact, many will do just what the minister said this afternoon; knowing that through their participation certificates they will benefit from any further rise of price many of them will be quite willing to deliver their wheat if the price is at all reasonable.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Is not the experience
exactly the opposite?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
No; they will wait and take whatever profit there may be on the participation certificates. If that is not true the whole purpose of this pool bill is removed. These people want to get 60 cents from the pool or cooperative and then take any other benefit that comes along. The same will be true under the wheat board.
The minister says that the main reason for not carrying on the wheat board as a permanent policy is the same reason that

caused the wheat pool to stop in 1929, and points to the loss last fall, which he puts at $48,000,000, although the Minister of Finance provided for only $25,000,000. I do not think any person can say the loss is $48,000,000, because that wheat has not yet been disposed of. Just now the market looks promising.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Even if it is $25,000,-
000 the same argument applies.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Yes, there
may be a loss. But had the wheat board been allowed to operate in 1936 and 1937 there might have been a profit; and they might have had a reserve fund to meet this loss.
The next thing the minister gives as a reason is that this $25,000,000 to $48,000,000 went to the wrong people, those who needed it least. There the minister is confusing two things. You cannot confuse relief for people who have no crop with marketing assistance for people who have a crop. When the minister's acreage bonus plan comes down, then we shall be talking about relief, but now we are dealing with marketing. You cannot expect a man who has a crop to produce for less than cost in order to do something for the man who has no crop. I still contend that, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said this afternoon, all the things the minister has said that we want to do we can do under the Wheat Board Act and do much better than under this bill.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Might I make a suggestion?
I do not know that this is the time to discuss the Wheat Board Act, but my hon. friend has been continually asking why the wheat board should not be continued as a permanent institution. One answer that I would give to that is that it was inaugurated by the former government in the first place to deal with an emergency. I do not think it was ever intended for anything else.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: It was intended as a permanent thing.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
I disagree with my hon.
friend. Then a royal commission was appointed to make a report on the whole situation.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext: By this government.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Yes, by this government.
That commission reported and recommended that the government get out of the wheat business and encourage the formation of pools, which is what is being provided for by the legislation introduced by my colleague.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
That is not
a reason for the government doing it.

35S3
Cooperative Wheat Marketing

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
1 should think that is a
very good reason.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OF INITIAL PAYMENT BY COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS OR ELEVATOR COMPANIES
speechtext:
I intended to speak on
the principle of this bill on second reading, but I was told by the whip that we should have an opportunity in committee. I wished to raise the principle of section 3 before Easter, when the minister spoke for two and three quarter hours and then moved the adjournment of the debate so that no opposition could be presented.
In my opinion, under section 3, initial payments paid to selling agencies, and the decision of the minister to be final, this is nothing from beginning to end but a political bill. I do not wish to delay the close of the session, I should like to see it closed before the king comes. But the opposition should have proper opportunity to present their views, and I wish to present my views for a few minutes, because ever since I came to the house in 1921 I have taken an interest in and made a study of the grain growing industry. I helped a great newspaper to spend a large sum of money for a survey on the prairies to find out the facts about this industry.
So far as I am concerned I am absolutely opposed to the principle of the bill as set out in the explanatory note. The explanatory note has to be read along with section 3. One notes from the last section that the bill is to come into force on a date to be fixed by proclamation. In other words, this is simply the first of a series of Santa Claus bills. Before Easter the minister said these bills could be read together and we could present our views in opposition to all the bills at the one time. I do not wish to delay the committee, but I believe the principles underlying all these bills are entirely wrong. Hon. gentlemen opposite condemned the late leader of the party to which I belong in connection with his wheat policy, although he knew more about the grain industry than the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and all his staff put together. Mr. Bennett utilized the credit of the whole country to hedge the grain and saved the country from bankruptcy at a critical time, which I believe was far better than the minister's half-baked schemes.
Last night the hon. member for Parry Sound referred to the "old gang." Well, Mr. Chairman, I could tell him something about the old free trade grain gang, both within and without this house that ran the grain business on the prairies-the free traders and their allies. That old gang is still in business; some of them have been canvassing and lobbying me for the past four weeks here in connection
with these bills. The minister was a free trader on the prairies, but now he is the most advanced protectionist in the country. He wants to give this industry more protection than it is given in any other country to-day. I agree that it is in the interests of the whole country to have agreement in regard to this great national industry, because, after all, the grain business is linked up with the railway business and the railway and banking problems. Hon. members to my left said they hoped to get some of our foreign markets back. Let me say to them they will never be able to do that, or get back what we lost. 1 do not wish to be unfair to the minister, who has a hard proposition to handle, but he is proceeding on the wrong basis.
Hon. gentlemen opposite condemned the late leader of this party for issuing blank cheques. What is this but a blank cheque? And then we give the minister power to bring the bill into force by proclamation. What is the wheat policy of this government? No one knows; it is here to-day and gone to-morrow, a policy of fits and starts and nothing long. Where is the money to come from to pay for this pegging, these bonuses, subventions and subsidies? It will come from the industrial workers of the two central provinces who compose over 50 per cent of the population of this country. Their income and sales taxes will pay for this bonus for one section of the country at the expense of others.
It is said that this legislation is being brought in to implement one of the recommendations contained in the Turgeon report, but it goes much further and deals with matters not mentioned in the report at all. Why was not section 3 of this bill referred to the law courts? This is a form of insurance, as are all these bonuses, subventions and all that sort of thing. The government asks the industrial workers to wait until the report of the Rowell commission is presented. The 'briefs presented to that commission by the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta all made reference to the very subject matter of this grain bonus legislation. If it was a good thing that the industrial workers, 51 per cent of our population, who have to pay the shot for this sort of thing, should be asked to wait for the report of the Rowell commission, why should it not be a good thing also to ask those engaged in agriculture to wait for the same thing?
When first I came into the house I introduced resolutions dealing with this very question of aid to agriculture, but at that time members from the west believed in free trade and the law of supply and demand. Now,
Cooperative Wheat Marketing

however, they have dropped that; now they want stabilization, bonuses, pegging and so on. In my opinion there is another way of meeting the situation, along the lines suggested by Mr. Bennett. I believe it would be far better and it would cost less and be a long range policy to nationalize agriculture than to have the system now proposed, which the Minister of Finance says will cost the country $25,000,000. I believe it will cost from $50,000,000 to $75,000,000, or if such an emergency as war should arise the cost may run to $100,000,000. The chief difficulty, as I see it, is to find a way to handle crops like wheat and com, of which we produce far more than we can consume under existing conditions. The obvious remedy, of course, is to increase the purchasing powers of the industrial workers to the point where they can consume more of our agriculture produce. Pending that happy day, however, the administration has a right to ask the farmers to assist by curtailing the production of those crops which cause most of the trouble. Why would it not be a good idea for the government to authorize definite steps along these lines:
1.	Buy directly from the farmer the wheat and corn needed for the domestic market at an adequate price, giving each farmer his proportion based on what he has been producing in recent years.
2.	Close the grain and cotton exchange and forbid all speculation in the necessities of life.
3.	Require millers, cotton manufacturers and other processors to buy what they need from the government.
4.	Permit the farmer who desires to produce more than his quota to sell his surplus in any market outside Canada. The government might even assist in forming cooperatives to facilitate such marketing, but it should not assume responsibility for the price received.
I realize, of course, that the farmer has the right to demand from the rest of us a fair reward for producing those things which we must have if we are to live. He should get that price, and no chiseling middleman or speculator should be allowed to deprive him of any part of it. The only way to assure that result is for Canada to do the entire job, from start to finish. If the farmer insists on producing more than is needed in this country he should be willing to take his chance in the world market.
That is very similar to the policy proposed by my late leader, who wanted to nationalize the grain crop in the grain bill of 1935 through a grain board. Hon. gentlemen opposite, then sitting in opposition

opposed it bitterly; they would not allow him to do that; they brought in an amendment to the grain bill, and made a great deal, both within and without the house, of talk about issuing blank cheques. This series of bills is in my opinion, worse than a blank cheque because they lead nowhere. The purpose of this legislation is said to be to assist in increasing the revenue of the farmers. We should not take these bills at their face value. It is proposed to guarantee a minimum price to primary producers who link themselves together in cooperative associations. According to this bill the initial price is not to exceed 60 cents. I think Mr. McFarland did splendid work for the people of Canada, under conditions of economic emergency, and when the orderly marketing of wheat was most necessary. He met with great difficulties in a world that was topsyturvy with over-production, loss of markets, over-acreage and falling prices. Mr. Bennett saved this country from bankruptcy by hedging grain at the head of the lakes. He brought great credit to the country. The industry was supported, and Canada was saved from bankruptcy. It was most fortunate then that with that huge surplus the price went up, and Canada was saved a loss of $150,000,000. That saving was brought about because of vision, and a careful handling by a man who understood the grain trade.
It was thought that the emergency would not be of long duration. Unfortunately, on account of greater uncertainty and greater difficulty, in these days of 1939 the outlook is still cloudy and unpromising, and I have great doubts and fears as to the possibility of any long-term adjustments. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has said we want a long-term policy. He is now going to have the wheat board competing with the pools and the cooperatives. How he is going to handle it, I do not know-in view of the falling prices, and with France, Germany and Italy off the market growing a big acreage, thus eliminating nearly one-third of what we generally send overseas of our exportable surplus.
The future is cloudy. It is fortunate that in 1935 the Conservative government did not listen to the clamouring and agitations that were then made. The minister at first suggested that the government should remain out of the grain trade completely. Then the policy was changed and the grain board retained. This policy of pegging and bonuses and subventions was supposed to be only temporary, and it was thought that the gov-vernment could in time get out of the business altogether, because in reality we have power to act only in an emergency.

Cooperative Wheat Marketing
This is only a Santa Claus bill, a political bill, introduced to tide the government over the next election. It may run into a loss of money, and particularly to the National railways. The minister has provided for a grand total deficit of $55,000,000; and to that amount must be added $25,000,000 which can be traced to these Santa Claus bills. And before the government is through it may go to $55,000,000 or $100,000,000. I say it is simply a bad gamble. The Minister of Finance figured that $25,000,000 would cover the expenditure. AVhere is the money to come from? Who is going to pay it? It must come out of income tax; it must come out of the sales tax. It will be taken from the industrial worker, and from the farmers of Ontario and Quebec who do not get five cents worth of protection.
I was canvassed by some of the lobbyists down here. I never saw such a lobby in my life-and I have been in Washington-as has been going on in this building in the last three or four weeks. Premiers and others from the prairies have been lobbying members of parliament and ministers to fix the price at 40 cents, 50 cents, 70 cents, 80 cents, or whatever it may be. As the minister acts the part of Santa Claus, it puts me in mind of Christmas and Santa Claus, and in mind of little Jack Horner sitting in his corner eating his Christmas pie. He puts in his thumb and pulls out a plum and says, "Oh, what a good boy am I."
Let me say to hon. members opposite that if this is the policy they are going to follow, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) will have to double his sales tax and his income tax. A few days ago I saw the line-up of poor working people-old people and younger people-paying their income tax. In Toronto they will have to pay for all this hand-out.
I hope I may be pardoned if I speak a little longer than I had intended, although I know we are in committee. However, we were told we could speak in committee, and if that were the procedure the bills might pass more quickly. As I have said, I do not wish to delay the session; in fact, I should like to see parliament prorogue at the end of next week. I am not joining to-night in that noble army of martyrs who wish to keep us here next June and July when the temperature is running 95 degrees in the shade.
The whole policy of the government is wrong, and if we support that policy there will be no end to it. May I ask the minister this question: Why did he not accept the policy offered by the government of the United States with regard to the orderly marketing of wheat on the north American
continent? He has said nothing about it. The department of agriculture at Washington asked the Canadian government to meet them to discuss the question of the carry-over. That carry-over will get worse as time goes on. We know this pegging business is in its infancy, but it will never be abandoned. Once they get their feet into the treasury down here, it will be a continuing offence. From an economic point of view it is wrong, and it is opposed to everything which hon. members who used to come from the prairies proposed. They will bankrupt the country. If these moneys were to go to the poor man who grows the grain I would not say anything about it. But it is in contradiction to the principle of confederation-each for all and all for each. No east and west about mel The people of the east have done their duty. There is a warm feeling in Ontario towards the people in want in the west. We can remember that a few years ago western people criticized people of the east for opposing legislation. We are not opposing aid in an emergency. I would say that people east of the great lakes have been better friends to the farmer on the prairie than have some of the hon. members opposite and some of the free trade premiers of the prairie provinces.
People from the east suffered in flesh and blood in the northwest rebellion. I remember not long ago reading where a regiment from Toronto went to the Northwest Territories, and, while there, saw one of the first wheat crops in that part of the country at Fish Creek. They went out to the west, across the lakes, when the temperature was 60 degrees below zero-and they do not now get a copper of pension. Why, they cannot get even a pension from this country; men who suffered thus cannot now get even a pension.

A central selling agency may be set up under the first two definitions
of the bill, which read:
(a)	"cooperative association" means an association of primary producers having for its object the marketing, under a cooperative plan, of wheat grown by the aforesaid primary producers;
(b)	"cooperative plan" means an agreement entered into by primary producers for the marketing, on a collective basis, of the whole or any part of the wheat grown by such producers in any crop year.
A cooperative plan would apply either in the case of an association composed entirely of producers or in the case of elevator companies organizing themselves into a pool. If the farmers of western Canada desire to do so and organize all three provinces into pools, they would have full control over the organization of their own central selling agency. On the other hand, if the elevator companies at the same time organized on a cooperative plan to handle grain, they would have a central selling agency of their own or they would appoint a producers' organization as a central selling agency to sell their grain. If the producers had an organization of their own the farmer would make his choice whether he wanted to sell through an organization entirely his own or through an organization partly controlled by the elevator people.
