Agricultural Products-Marketing

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext: I have listened with great interest to the brief explanation of this bill by the minister. He related this bill somewhat to the Natural Products Marketing Act, which, he says, was declared ultra vires shortly after the present administration came into office. First I criticize the administration for waiting until the dying days of this session, four years after the Natural Products Marketing Act was declared ultra vires, before passing legislation which, he now says, is designed to carry out some of the provisions of that legislation, and assist organizations which were built up under that act.

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext: What did you do about it?

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext:
We kept it in effect as long as we were in office.
The heading of this bill declares that it is "an act to assist and encourage cooperative marketing of agricultural products." I say frankly and honestly that so far as this bill will assist agriculture I am very much in agreement with it. Under this bill the definition of an agricultural product seems to include nearly every kind of product, except wheat, that is grown on the farms of Canada. So I suppose the bill is intended to apply to all lines of agricultural production. Certainly the mixed farming industry of Canada is desperately in need of some aid in its marketing problem, because marketing continues to be the major problem which faces agriculture in this dominion.
There are a number of reasons for that. The unit of production on the farms of Canada is small. Under modern conditions it is practically impossible for the individual farmer to process and distribute his product. As a result of this there has gradually grown up throughout the dominion, as in other countries, a lucrative and thriving business carried on by organizations which collect, process and distribute the farmer's product. Unfortunately there has developed at the same time a gradual widening of the spread between producer and consumer prices. When the farmer's product leaves his hands, it may, in many instances, be regarded as raw material. Its transformation into consumer goods necessitates costs of collection, of manufacture or processing, freight to the ultimate market, commissions to dealers and commission men, or profits made by those who are handling farm products to the consumer. In many instances, because of these costs the farmer gets a much smaller share of the consumer's dollar than that which goes to the middleman. This condition has grown up through the years.
I have said already that the farming industry is composed of small individual units, and for that reason the individual farmer has little or no bargaining power. He has to accept for his goods prices which are set or determined by a great number of factors, and rapid and violent fluctuations in the prices he receives are constantly taking place. The farmer has to make his plans at least a year before his goods are ready for market, and in the interval prices which were adequate when his plans were made often drop far below the cost of production by the time the goods are sold. Much of the farmer's products, such as milk and fruit and vegetables, are perishable and must be marketed immediately ; his live stock must be sold at a certain stage in their development otherwise they deteriorate and the cost of carrying them in the hope of higher prices is excessive. So it seems apparent to even the casual student that the first and great need of the farmer is price stability.
I am sorry that I cannot see in this bill a solution of the farmer's marketing problem. I have already said that so far as it is a solution and so far as it will benefit the farmer I am in agreement with it. But there is in this bill little if any provision whereby agriculture as a whole will secure what is most necessary, namely, the power of collective bargaining. I am afraid that this bill has been brought in at the present time more as a gesture to influence the votes of the mixed farming industry in Canada on the eve of an election than for any other reason. Any scheme which will permanently benefit the dairy industry, the live stock industry, poultry raising or any other line of farming, should be comprehensive in its scope. No small group of farmers organized into a cooperative association can prevent price fluctuation, nor can they keep farm prices in line with costs of production-and by that I mean costs of efficient production-unless it be in some branch of agriculture which is local or where production is comparatively small.
The whole scheme which is proposed in this bill, and also in the bill for bonusing cheese, seems to me haphazard, piecemeal and ineffective. No doubt the minister feels that because of the assistance which is to be given to the western wheat growers, as outlined in the bill just passed and in a number of others which are now before the house, some consideration should also be given to the mixed farmers of Canada. Undoubtedly they are desperately in need of assistance to solve their marketing problem. But it is to be regretted that the minister did not give greater



Agricultural Products-Marketing
consideration to his proposals before advancing them in this bill and the bill to bonus cheese; for even the most casual observer must admit that such assistance as these bills offer will be entirely inadequate, and their futility leaves the minister and the government open to the suspicion that these measures are purely political in their inception and effect, as I think the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) stated earlier in the evening.
Any scheme for the marketing of farm products must, in my opinion, be broad and comprehensive enough to control a sufficient percentage of any given product to influence and govern its price. It should be sufficiently powerful and should have adequate machinery to lift our surpluses of domestic products off the market and dispose of them without depressing domestic prices. To this end I believe some system should be set up in this country to deal with surpluses of farm products. Such a system should be broad enough not only to finance the removal of these surpluses from the market but also to see that the highest possible quality in any given line of farm products is shipped into the markets of the world. Unless and until some such scheme is devised and carried out, measures of the sort we are now discussing will be abortive and will not accomplish the end we have in mind, an end I am sure everyone desires to see attained.
I want it distinctly understood that in proposing such a scheme as, we will say, an export board, or some other organization to lift these surpluses off the market, I am expressing my own views entirely. I believe, however, that such a board should and could operate in conjunction with these cooperative associations which probably will be set up sooner or later under this scheme. These associations, by means of advertising and in other ways, may help the farmer to direct his production into the lines best calculated to yield the greatest return and eliminate these unmanageable surpluses. I think it has already been demonstrated beyond question that if too much butter is manufactured, the whole dairy industry suffers. On the other hand it is also apparent that our hogs are often marketed in a way that is detrimental to the industry. During certain periods of the year hogs come out too readily; during other periods there is a scarcity, and as a result there is altogether too much fluctuation in price.
It seems to me that a number of other matters must be considered before a workable scheme for the marketing of farm products

can be carried out in this country. I do not wish to delay the second reading of this bill. I simply repeat that I think measures of this kind will be impotent and futile unless something further is done, and that they may result in worse confusion than we have at the present time. Any further remarks I have to make I will leave until the bill is in committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is another of the bills dealing with agriculture brought into this house in the dying days of the session. No doubt this is a most important and conspicuous piece

Agricultural Products-Marketing
of legislation. It is important because it deals with an industry that is fundamental to any hope of prosperity in this dominion, that is essential to any security for the empire either in peace or in war. It is important because to-day we are challenged in the marketing of our surplus products by changed world conditions.
It is not my desire to delay this house at any great length, because no one is more desirous than I am of concluding this session in time to give a proper welcome to Their Majesties the King and Queen. But, Mr. Speaker, a problem ten years old, an issue that has been before the people of Canada for such a long time, a problem which this government promised to solve, should not have been left by this floundering government until the eleventh hour.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext:
My hon.
friends opposite laugh; the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) smiles. Oh, yes; he has been here a long time, and I trust that he may live a long time yet. He is one of the most delightful men in public life to-day, but I say to him that after the next election I think he will be asking me how my government is getting along.
To continue, Mr. Speaker, I say this measure is conspicuous because of its introduction at this time, and also because it gives the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) more power than it gives hope to the agriculturists of this country. It does not even analyse the problem, let alone offer a solution. I have no apology to offer for my position with reference to cooperative marketing in this dominion. Some of the older members in the house will recall that ten years ago I suggested to the government of the day, as I later suggested when my own party was in power, that the time had come when we should meet the problems of world competition and face the challenge presented to us as agriculturists by establishing an export marketing board to deal with the marketing of our export products. Agriculture has been long since in Canada a loss leader to a haphazard economy.
I am glad at this time that the government, even in these last days of the session, even in the last hours of the session, are turning their eyes at last towards the mixed farming problems of Canada. This is the eleventh hour-the dying days of the session. As the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. MacMillan) said the other night in another debate, if I may be pardoned for referring to
71492-226J
it:	"It is better to have a death-bed repentance than to have no repentance at all.1' Even he knew that this is the last time the government would have a chance to repent.
So I am glad to see that at last the Minister of Agriculture has turned his eyes towards that great, fundamental, basic feature of Canadian agriculture, namely, mixed farming in Canada. It is strange that we should have this hysterical stampede towards a solution, just before an election. He tries now to solve a problem which should have been solved long ago. Someone may say to me: "What about your party some years ago?" I say we tried to solve the problem, but that the party now in office found our panacea unconstitutional. If I were as good a lawyer as the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), I would question the constitutionality of the measure now before the house. But, Mr. Speaker, I have no apology to make for the policy which has been followed by the Conservative party. Two wrongs do not make a right.
This problem is ten years old. It has not been solved in the past. I say again, if it will bear repetition-and I know it will-that Canadian agriculture has been a loss leader to a haphazard prosperity in Canada, It has been a loss leader to a haphazard economy or, if you will, a haphazard depression-and I know whereof I speak. I believe I know the man on the back concession as well as does any other hon. member in the house. I know that in that circle of enterprise in the dominion there have been men and women who in the last few years have fought a battle such as people in no other enterprise in Canada have fought. I know of men who have worked to keep their families on $20 a month, men who have toiled from the rising to the setting of the sun, and for less wages than the amount that would be accepted by many men in the cities for relief. Had it not been for agriculture acting as a loss leader to Canadian prosperity, this country would be bankrupt to-day.
I realize present conditions do not offer much hope. Every hon. member within sound of my voice, every businessman in Canada, knows that Canadian agriculture has borne the brunt of the times. The bricklayer has quit his work and has joined the relief ranks because he can not get $1.25 an hour. But the farmer has toiled from five o'clock in the morning until seven o'clock or eight o'clock at night for $20 a month; and, in some instances, boarded himself and kept his family. His poor wife did not know what it was to have the fineries even of the wives of the men on relief. I know how men in that great

Agricultural Products-Marketing
old historic province of Quebec have sacrificed in these times of depression more than has been necessary at any time since the great war.
At the present time the distress signal is flying from the bam of almost every farm in Canada simply because we have had a government that has failed and has been unprepared to deal effectively with the problem. And when I speak of the problem and about conditions now prevailing in Canada among the farmers, I do not for one moment say that they are paupers or that they are in any way an economic menace. I know those people; I know them to be jealous of their independ-ance. They are thrifty, industrious, resourceful, strong, virile and ready to meet any situation which may arise. It is not always lack of ability or effort on their part that is :esponsible for their condition. Some of the hardest working farmers are to-day the worst off. The fact remains, however, that in the present state of affairs, a state of affairs which cannot be ignored much longer, if we are going to make agriculture the subject of a federal subsidy to be supported by taxes from the treasury of this dominion then it is only reasonable to expect the dominion government to find markets for surplus products. If we are going to consider Canadian agriculture there must be a frank realization that while wheat is a tremendously important crop in Canada, no longer can we live by wheat and wheat alone.
To-day little more than one-third of our wheat crop is consumed at home; the bulk is exported from the dominion. It is true that sales abroad mean wealth to the people of Canada. In the past few years there has oeen a contraction of the export market for this great Canadian commodity, and that contraction has affected not only the growers out the prosperity of the dominion as a whole. To-day, however, we must realize that the channels of international trade are broken in many places. International credits have been suspended. Trade has been abused and restricted by quotas, licences, barter agreements, controlled currency and other impediments which check trade channels and financial and commercial enterprise. Under these circumstances I believe the only thing to do is for us to put our house in order. Consideration must be given to other branches of agriculture, but we must direct our attention to a national policy of substitution for rather than subsidization of products which we can neither sell nor consume. The bountiful Canadian wheat crop of years gone by, the excellent world prices, coasting along with

world prosperity, seem to have created in Canada a wheat-minded approach to agricultural problems.
May I remind hon. members that the value of our wheat production in Canada in the last ten years has been between only 18 per cent and 20 per cent of the total agricultural production. I have been in the house for fifteen or sixteen sessions, and from the beginning to the end of that time I have heard nothing but wheat, wheat, wheat-morning to night-wheat in the committee on agriculture-wheat in the House of Commons; one would imagine it was the only problem that people engaged in agriculture had to face.

But I say
we have kept you fellows alive. Many of your citizens would have starved to death had it not been for our people in eastern Canada. I say in all fairness that we started you in western Canada, and we survive you. I say we produce five times as much in agricultural products as do the wheat producers of this dominion; let there be no misunderstanding about that. Let us face the facts. We have been wheat-minded; we have been wheat-conscious. We have imagined we controlled the bread-basket of the world. But I say to you that for ten years western Canada has not produced 20 per cent of the total agricultural production of this dominion. We in the east have maintained the security of Canada, in mixed farming production.

There is no quarrel
with that.

speechtext: There is no quarrel with that. The only sound basis for agriculture in any country that has survived the days of exploitation of the fertile soil of pioneer states is the development of mixed farming. Do no let us have any misunderstanding about that. Wheat is an important asset. I come from an agricultural family and I have grown wheat; I grew more wheat last year per acre than any of my friends to my left grew from three acres.

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext: How many bushels?

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext:
I am not boasting, but I am interested in wheat production, and I realize that one cannot rob the soil continually and expect to produce good crops. The fact that I produced fifty bushels to the acre last year was as a result of feeding the soil rather than robbing it.

Agricultural Products-Marketing
No country has sustained a successful agriculture without handing back to the soil something of what you rob from it.
Every country in the world in the last few years has changed its economy. From Scandinavia in the north to Italy in the south we have seen import restrictions imposed, land reform, bonused production, and other devices which have changed the whole front of the wheat market of the world. A greater degree of self-sufficiency seems to be considered sound economics in the different countries of the world to-day. Security of supply in the face of a possible world crisis seems to have been the dominant factor in the policy of Germany and Italy and even the old land herself. Europe has almost ceased to buy our wheat, and we are challenged to find new markets and substitutes for our wheat. State after state, faced with the problem of disposing of its surpluses, have established virtual monopolies in marketing services with the whole resources of the country behind them.
We have now before us Bill No. 89. I am not going to censure the Minister of Agriculture for introducing this bill. I know he is trying to do something. Heaven knows that after four years in power, and now facing the people, he would at last try to do something. But I wish to point out to him that the venture of this dominion to control the world price of wheat a few years ago did not succeed. The coffee venture of Brazil to control the price was not very successful a few years ago. The control of cotton prices in the United States was not very successful a few years ago. Now we have before us a bill which will not solve the problem. Costly and ineffective price-fixing systems, to be applied to local conditions, cannot be undertaken without adding to the load of the already over-burdened taxpayers. The money necessary to guarantee minimum prices and to make grants in aid will certainly come eventually from the farmers by visible or invisible taxation.
This is typical pre-election legislation, a bid to everyone, a gesture to all. This bill vests in the minister power to make regulations governing its operation. For example, the minister, and the minister alone, can say where and how the statute shall be applied. He, and he alone, may make regulations prescribing the manner in which the average price for a product shall be ascertained. The minister, and the minister alone, may establish the proportion of primary producers in any one geographical area the products of which are to be marketed under a plan of a guaranteed
initial price. The minister and the minister alone, shall decide the proportion of an agricultural product, in any designated area, that shall be marketed under a system of a guaranteed initial price. The minister, and the minister alone, shall decide the time or times when payment subsequently to the initial payment shall be made. The minister, and the minister alone, is given full authority to extend or withhold the legislation if and when he sees fit.
This bill is nothing more or less than a blank cheque for the minister to fill out in expedient rations as he sees fit. It substitutes government- by arbitrary will for government by law.
The purpose of Bill No. 89 is to guarantee to primary producers who bind themselves into a cooperative association an initial price for their products not to exceed 80 per cent of the average wholesale price of such products over the three years preceding the year of production, and if, on account of uncontrollable conditions, the market price obtained for such products falls below the established minimum figure, the difference will be made up by the treasury. When the market price is higher than the guaranteed initial price, the producers in the cooperative association are to share in the surplus.
Under this bill, worn-out acres will compete with fertile soil; the scrawny and thin hog will compete with the fat and finished hog; the diseased tree will compete with the healthy tree; and the market will be flooded with inferior crops, all of which will be harder to dispose of, bringing a lower price and accordingly demanding a greater share of this peculiar federal assistance.
A few of the needs of agriculture may be alleviated by intelligent legislative control but by and large the salvation of the farmei is to be worked out in one spot alone, and by one person alone, namely, the farmer himself on his farm. The biggest thing this government can do is to help the farmer to h Ip himself, by assisting him, not only to produce better products but to market them in better ways to meet world competition.

What have my friends opposite done for the home market? They have allowed foreign countries to build up their markets instead of helping us to build up our home market here.
The soundness of a policy such as is incorporated in the bill is questionable because it is a policy that puts all the

Agricultural Products-Marketing
emphasis on a fixed price at home instead of upon quality abroad. It may be good politics in an election year to guarantee a local price at home, but it would be better economics to guarantee a national quality abroad?
This bill provides for government by individuals rather than government by law. It is an effort to "goose-step" the individual to an election tune rather than organize the nation to meet a world challenge. It is "tail wag dog" economics, fixing prices not by the law of supply and demand, not by quality, not by service, but by the arbitrary will of this new political Prince of the Prairies, who now asks this house for a blank cheque on a treasury that is struggling under a fifty million dollar overdraft. In the wake of this "new comic form of political genius" we can anticipate more wasteful expenditure in the future, more unbalanced budgets, and heavier deferred debts for our children and our children's children.
And now with our Minister of Agriculture and the government facing an election year, without any proper or sound diagnosis of the case we have before us this "gunshot" prescription of a political doctor in an election year, in an effort to save a floundering government. This bill does nothing to solve the very crux of the problem. I ask any lion, member within the sound of my voice who knows anything about agriculture in Canada to tell me what it does to standardize quality in the markets overseas. Will the minister himself tell me that?

How long do	you	expect him tocarry on	and to	save	this	country from
collapse? He has saved it through the most difficult years of its existence. We must meet him part way.
When I asked the Minister of Agriculture what he had done to standardize our agriculture in world markets, he said it was done under another bill. Surely there are no more bills coming. Why are they brought in during the dying hours of the session? Why were they not brought in years ago?

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext: What has been done to meet world competition? The Minister of Agriculture changes his policy from day to day. He raises his ante in election bids from week to week, and now asks for a blank cheque in order that he may homestead on the back concessions, looking in election year for votes at home rather than for markets abroad.

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext: We have no concessions in our part of the country.

speechtext: Are you against the bill?

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext:
We cannot expect, by giving the minister any such arbitrary powers, to restore the levels of farm incomes. We need an aggressive and consistent national policy which recognizes the difficulties and complications of changed national and international conditions. We must give first consideration to home markets for our own farmers. Surely there is no one who will disagree with me when he realizes that we in this country consume approximately 85 per cent of all that we produce. The greatest market for agriculture is the home market. Therefore we must foster our home market first. Then there are the secondary markets for our surplus foodstuffs, particularly within the British empire.
There is a feeling in Canada to-day that our government must offer subsidies to our farmers. I have no strenuous objections to that, provided the subsidies are in the national interest and are made under a defined national plan, and provided the federal treasury can afford to make expenditures of this type. I believe it is important for the government to make certain that the investment shows some sign of returns in prospect. Some years ago I suggested that we should have a national export board in Canada and that we should have a bonus policy for high grade products so that they could be placed on the markets of the world in competition with the rest of the world. Perhaps my suggestion fell on deaf ears. But it seems to me that the present policy of the government is to stay on the back concession lines and bid for the support of men under local conditions rather than meet world conditions.
If we are to embark upon a policy of farm subsidies the government, I submit, should plan to give some consideration to the following requirements. It should give some consideration to a diversified and intensified agriculture, not to wheat alone. It should give some consideration to soil improvement. Inducements should be offered to farmers who put a larger proportion of their acreage into legumes and fertility restoring crops. Improvement payments should be forthcoming to farmers who take measures to prevent further destruction of the soil by erosion. Inducements could be offered to farmers to produce products which Canada now imports from other countries, because we do import considerably from other countries. Despite the fact that we are floundering along, trying to find markets overseas, we import thousands of head of cattle and thousands of dollars worth of animal fats. Some consideration should be given to the transference of marketable crops into industrial consumption. But what this country needs more than anything else is a national export plan to sell our surplus products on the markets of the world in face of organized international competition.
These suggestions would require no coercion or control. Farmers would simply have the choice of taking advantage of the inducements or of following their usual routines in accordance with modern supply and demand.
It is questionable whether we can offer the farmers of Canada permanent relief through any process of purchasing their surplus crops and holding those surpluses as threats over future crops.
A national export board rather than a local control board is justified at the present time. We must meet world challenges rather than consider domestic expediency. We must face new problems in new ways; we must meet national challenges with national policies. New nationalized marketing policies of almost every supply country in the world constitute a practical competitive condition such as Canada has not been forced to meet before on the export market. This militant competition of state-directed marketing monopolies has already demonstrated its ingenuity and efficiency in world markets. We, therefore, must find a sound, sane and comprehensive plan to distribute our surplus products more systematically in face of this new form of state-assisted competition.
Local organizations, inspection and different forms of competition are all important for our domestic markets. But may I suggest that they are more or less provincial, in authority and in constitution. I believe it is the responsibility of the dominion government to coordinate provincial organizations towards a greater nationalized plan to dispose of our surplus products.

Agricultural Products-Marketing
The bonuses, subsidies or subventions which may be necessary must be directed nationally to encourage in our agricultural export products higher quality, more standardized grade and greater regularity of supply.
Our agriculture has been haphazard in the past and it has now become local. It is sectional so far as western wheat is concerned; it is seasonal for the live stock producers in the east. It has grown to be almost political. We must encourage mixed farming by means of a national policy applicable to all parts of Canada, designed to stabilize prices in our great domestic market through the necessary national export assistance which we now know is so essential to meet the new form of competition in world markets. It is all very well in these last days of the session to let things go by the board and to neglect those issues that touch the very heart of Canadian prosperity. Do hon. members realize that even in old England they have spent $40,000,000 to subsidize agriculture? Do they realize that in Italy and Germany, indeed in all the old countries of Europe, the governments have had bonus policies and have endeavoured by every means possible to make their countries self-sustaining? They have introduced a nationalized export policy with the result that to-day we in this dominion are faced with a situation such as we have never had to contend with in the past. Do hon. members know where Canada will sell its wheat in the future?

Yes, I am against the bill. I am against the bill because it is a goose-stepping plan for the individual rather than one to meet world competition. The minister should know, and if he does not there are in the gallery a number of officials from his own department who would tell him that our first duty in this dominion in the interest of agriculture is to find a way to meet world competition, to get rid of our agricultural surpluses rather than dance our people to an election tune to win votes. We must find means of placing our agricultural surplus. Every country in the world has subsidized its exports, and I will support the Minister of Agriculture in any legislation he brings down to establish an export marketing board and give a bonus-which will cost much less than this measure-to high grade quality only, equal to the best quality produced anywhere in the world, for that market. If he does that he will start at the right end, the economic end, and I suggest that he do that instead of playing politics.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): The oration just delivered by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) was most interesting. Of course something was hurt; I do not say someone, it did not hurt any one of our colleagues but I fear the hon. member hurt his desk badly by banging it so loudly and so many times. He spoke at length of "loss leaders" and also repeated the expression that we used to hear from the lips of his lamented former leader, "those within the sound of my voice." He repeated that so often that it probably gave him the illusion that he was someone other than himself.
There are of course great experts in agriculture in all countries of the world. I had the privilege of listening to one in England, the Right Hon. Mr. Morrison, a remarkable man who is now Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. I heard him prescribe two diets, one for peace-time and one for time of war. The peace-time diet was meat and the wartime diet was wheat. As the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has no interest in wheat and probably is a great admirer of Mr. Morrison, who was a prominent Tory in England, it may mean that as we shall have no exclusive wheat diet for some time we shall have peace. As the wheat diet is the diet for war and as the hon. member is not for it, we shall have peace and a meat diet. This is just as serious as what the hon. gentleman has said.

I am glad the hon. gentleman says "hear, hear," because I have spoken lightly for two or three minutes in answer to him. But now I want to speak seriously; probably he will not see the difference, but that is of no importance because I do not try to convince him. I want to speak seriously about a grave problem in this country. Of course, when one lives in a rural district, meets the farmers and is interested in their needs, their difficulties and their progress, he can learn a great deal if he is willing to learn.
It is true that in our part of the country, in the eastern provinces, we have mixed farming. Most of the farmers there have the spirit of pioneers. And there are some of them who deserve even more credit than the ordinary farmer; they are the settlers who clear the bush in order to cultivate the land. The farmers of eastern Canada, having the spirit of pioneers, at first did not lean on any government for help. They -were making their own roads and carrying on their affairs without any subsidy or any help. But with the coming of harder times they have had to rely to a certain extent on government assistance, and their point of view now is that what

Agricultural Products-Marketing
is done for one part of the country should be done for other parts. If it is good for one section of the country it must be good for the other; that is their point of view. May I repeat something that you, Mr. Speaker, know very well; it is that the farmers of eastern Canada deserve as much help as those of the west. And the situation is not always agreeable for them. They strive hard, they have difficulty, and they expect someone to come to their assistance.
Of course under the British North America Act agriculture and immigration are, in the first place, provincial matters. The dominion and the provinces have joint jurisdiction in those two fields only. As time went on, there were many changes, and little by little the dominion has been doing more with regard to agriculture by way of experimental farms and by assisting farmers. I wonder what is the practical difference in the way the dominion and provincial departments of agriculture are operated. It must be very slight. Would it not be better to keep the experimental farms and illustration stations throughout the country under the administration of the dominion government and then give the provinces a subsidy, in proportion to their population, which subsidy would be under the control of the provincial governments? Then no one could complain that more was done for one section of the country than for another.
Further, I wonder if the creation of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan was in fact a good thing. There is no doubt that Sir Wilfrid Laurier meant very well; he wanted to see this country larger and more populous, but now that the western provinces are costing Canada so much by way of loans, grants and guarantees I wonder if in regard to the dominion these western provinces do not occupy the same position that Newfoundland occupied with regard to England, and if it would not be better to return those provinces to the territories they once were, with a commissioner in charge. That would be a simple way of managing the business of those provinces. A petition could be addressed to the imperial parliament requesting the repeal of the Westminster statutes that were passed thirty-three years ago. Then those provinces would be in the same position as Newfoundland, until their prosperity was restored. I wonder if that would not be a good thing. They would have a fine territory; they would be happy and contented and they could try their own experiments.

So I would say that anything that can be done to maintain the wheat industry of western Canada, and to prevent the farmers of the west from being forced into some other line of endeavour, is in the interests of eastern agriculture.
While the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe was speaking, I looked up the figures in regard to the production of one commodity in which Ontario and Quebec are interested, namely, butter. I found that in 1937 Saskatchewan produced 23,000,000 pounds of butter, with a home consumption of between

I will answer that question in a moment. Ontario showed a .production of 81.500,000 pounds, with a consumption of 92,000,000 pounds; Quebec produced
74.000.	000 pounds and consumed 88,000,000 pounds, while the three maritime provinces had a production of 11,500,000 pounds and a consumption of 20,250,000 pounds. So in 1937 the production of eastern Canada was 33,000,000 pounds short of the consumptive requirements. In 1938 production in the prairies was increased by 6,000,000 pounds; in Ontario, by 5.500,000; in Quebec, by 4,500,000

pounds, and in the maritimes, by 2,000,000 pounds. That brought up our production to some 12,000,000 pounds more than we needed in this country. If our western farmers took the advice that is so frequently tendered in this house and went into the production of dairy products, I am not sure what some of the eastern dairy interests would do.
We have discussed wheat a great deal in this house. That is because, as I said earlier, to quote the former leader of the opposition- I have not his exact words under my hand, but I know what they were-wheat is Canada's greatest source of new wealth. He went on to say that since the west had been settled, something like $10,000,000,000 in new wealth had been produced in that way. It is true that during the last eight or nine years western Canada has suffered from drought and economic disaster, but that is no reason in the world why western Canada should be considered as a sort of poor relation of eastern Canada. When I look round the east and see the fine financial institutions, with their tremendous reserve funds marked on their windows, I know perfectly well that a great deal of that new wealth originated in western Canada in days gone by and that the people who produced it have precious little to show for the productive years that are now past.
I do not know a great deal about some matters covered by this particular bill because I have not given them special study, but I know western Canada will support any legislation that may be introduced in the interests of the eastern producer. The only thing I do know about this legislation is that 1 have heard it criticized because it is not considered sufficiently comprehensive. I found myself in complete agreement with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe in at least one particular; that was when he suggested that we ought to have a thorough economic survey made by those competent to conduct it. One thing I do regret is that such an act was on the statute books of this country and that in the first session of this parliament it was repealed by this government. So then all I wish to say is that I do not know the extent to which this bill is satisfactory to eastern agricultural interests, but I know that if it is as unsatisfactory as the wheat marketing legislation now before the house it will indeed be very unsatisfactory. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) is quite wrong if he thinks that the wheat bills are going to help the present government back into power. They will, on the contrary prevent their getting back into power, so far as western Canada is concerned.
(Mr. Coldwell.]
Mr. WILLIAM HAYHURST (Vegreville); Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the house more than to say that western Canada is certainly the treasure house of Canada. At least it is the treasure house of agricultural production, and is rich in oil wells and various other products. This bill of course deals with the marketing of products other than wheat, by cooperative methods. We know that men in western Canada and in other parts of the country have given the best of their lives to the development of cooperative industry. Upon those foundations which they properly laid we want to build. Therefore the idea of developing cooperative enterprise is very strong with us. It is a strong sentiment in western Canada.
Looking back upon my own life I know that when I first went to western Canada I was interested in the development of cooperative societies, wheat pools and so on. In our communities we had to develop various cooperative assistance, some of which fell by the wayside because of lack of confidence of the people, and some of which succeeded. 'If the people will not place their confidence in these movements they will always be a failure. In that respect we may take Great Britain as an example. They have developed various cooperative enterprises, and in many respects have been very successful. In a town in western Canada with which. I am familiar there is a cooperative enterprise which has been exceptionally successful, while in the next town the cooperative enterprise was not a success because the manager in that particular instance was not trustworthy. There must be proper management and confidence of the people.
If this bill will do anything to help agriculture, no matter whether it be in Quebec, Ontario, the maritimes, British Columbia or the prairie provinces, it will have our support. We realize that Canada must be developed as an entity, and when we speak of wheat we do so only because it is one of the great products of the dominion. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) spent about half his time talking about something he deplored, but if he had devoted that time to telling hon. members how cooperative enterprise could have been developed in milk production or cheese production I believe his observations would have been more constructive and more to the point.
The bill before the house deals with products other than wheat. In passing, I would add that it is not worded quite accurately. When I asked a little while ago if the measure would include cheese I was asking the question quite innocently, reading the bill as it was

I should certainly like to see developments in cooperative enterprise instead of in the bill. We must remember that most Canadian farmers are in a very difficult situation. They need support. It does not matter whether they are in the back concessions of Quebec or in my own constituency; they are worthy of such support. People living on the farms and doing the best they can are the back-bone of the country, and if we are not prepared to help them the country will naturally go to the dogs. But we are prepared to help those people, and hon. members in this corner of the house are prepared to cooperate with this or any other government for the welfare of the people of all of Canada.

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext: When I asked the minister on second reading why this measure did not include natural products as defined by the bill of 1934 he referred me to the Minister of Fisheries who, he said, was introducing a bill dealing with the matter. I would point out, however, that that bill is only in the resolution stage, and has been that way for ten days. If we are going to prorogue a week from to-morrow there is small chance of having it passed. Anyway, it deals only with salt fish and the export of salt fish. What I am referring to is the Natural Products Marketing Act assented to in 1934, which covered the products of agriculture, and of the forests, seas, lakes or rivers. I believe it is in order to ask why, if we are going into this system of cooperative marketing-and some people think it is desirable; I think it is-it should' be confined only to agriculture.

subsubtopic: OTHER THAN WHEAT-ENCOURACEMENT OF COOPERATIVE MARKETING BY GUARANTEEING INITIAL PAYMENT
speechtext:
The main reason, so far as fisheries are concerned, is the one I indicated when answering the hon. member previously. As the resolution indicates, a bill to deal with salt fish is being brought down. At the time the bill now before the committee was being drafted I did not have full information as to what the intention was in connection with that particular legislation. I should
think, however, that the proper place to add fish, other than salt fish, would be in that rather than in this legislation, because this has to do with farm products.
Then, so far as products of the forests are concerned, I understand there was a great deal of controversy at the time the Natural Products Marketing Act was discussed as to where the division should be made with respect to products of the forest. There was the question whether lumber of certain types, shingles and that sort of thing, should be included. We thought in drafting this bill that at this stage at least it was better to confine it to agricultural products, and to try it out experimentally for a year. If a year hence it is thought advisable to add other products I do not think there would be any serious objection, but at this time I think it would be best to try it out on agricultural products alone.

What other products has
the minister in mind which might possibly be included? I was surprised to hear the minister mention lumber, because it is far removed from wheat. Many other products would come in between the categories of agricultural products and lumber.

speechtext:
As at present drafted,
the bill is presumed to cover all agricultural products. The suggestion just made was that we should take in other products, other than those of the farm, namely that we should take in fish and products of the forests. I am just saying I do not think it is advisable in this bill, which is more or less of an experiment to try to promote cooperative marketing in connection with farm products, to include, in the present year, other natural products.
